title: Does it matter how we refer to individuals with substance-related conditions? A randomized study of two commonly used terms

claims.statement: In one pre-registered online experiment with adults who said they had no substance use or psychiatric diagnosis and knew of none in a close relative, the words used to describe a person's difficulty changed some of the attitudes readers reported, but not others, and changed what they did in a pretend money task only slightly. 1,613 adults (largest age group 18 to 25; 55.9% women; 77.1% White; recruited through university research-participation schemes, Prolific and social media; country of residence not stated) were each randomly assigned to read one short story about a person called Alex. When Alex's serious trouble at home and work was said to come from increasing drug use rather than from a health concern (819 against 741 readers), readers reported wanting more social distance from Alex (standardized difference d 0.87), saw Alex as more dangerous (d 0.78) and gave higher public-stigma scores (d 0.95; means 50.6 against 42.2): two of these differences are large by the usual standard and the third (danger) is just below it. They agreed less that the condition had genetic or disease causes (d −0.35), and their hope for Alex's recovery was the same within the study's equivalence bounds (d −0.06). In a pretend task in which readers could give or take small sums of money for Alex's answers, readers of the drug-use story took slightly more money (62.05 against 53.96 pence; d 0.14, interval 0.02 to 0.26), a difference the study could not show to be larger than its 0.20 threshold for a meaningful effect, and gave the same amount within the equivalence bounds (d −0.03). Among readers of the drug-use story, calling the condition a 'chronically relapsing brain disease' rather than a 'problem' (392 against 423) made readers agree more that it had genetic or disease causes (d 0.54; the study calls this subscale blame). With the brain-disease label, social distance (d −0.20, interval −0.36 to −0.03) and public stigma (−0.18, −0.34 to −0.02) were slightly lower, and the differences in danger (−0.11) and hope (−0.07) were smaller; all four were inconclusive, so the study could not tell whether any of them was more than trivial, and the label did not reliably change the money given or taken. Framing Alex's treatment as likely to succeed rather than uncertain (the two versions also differed in whether Alex was in a treatment programme or had seen a doctor) gave inconclusive differences on every attitude measure and on money given, and the same money taken (Pennington et al., 2023). The study measured attitudes reported after one made-up story, not how people who use drugs are actually treated by the public, health workers or services; people with a substance use or psychiatric diagnosis, or a close relative with one, could not take part; in the drug-use version four questionnaire items named opioids, so that comparison changed the questions as well as the story; the intervals printed as 99% match 98% intervals; and it did not compare person-first words with labels for the person. Words for the person were tested in one earlier, smaller experiment: of 728 people at talks on substance use at two mental-health conferences in 2008 (location not stated), 516 (mean age 51; 64.5% with a doctoral-level degree) completed one of two versions of a story about a man in court-ordered treatment who had positive drug and breath tests; those whose version called him 'a substance abuser' agreed slightly more with statements about blame, punishment and non-medical responses than those whose version said he had 'a substance use disorder' (2.92 against 2.82 on a 1–6 scale; d about 0.2), and did not differ detectably in willingness to have him as an employee, neighbour, co-worker or friend, or in treatment-related statements (Kelly & Westerhoff, 2010). That study calls itself randomized, but the two versions were handed out alternately; 29% of those handed a form did not complete it; its printed p = .02 matches an unstated one-sided test (two-sided about .04, above the authors' own threshold of .025); and it could not rule out differences of about the same size in social contact or treatment statements. Certainty: low. Status: single study.
claims.magnitude: Pennington et al. (2023), Cohen's d with intervals printed as 99% that match 98% intervals (card reporting issue): drug use vs health concern (819 vs 741): social distance 0.87 (0.74 to 0.99), perceived danger 0.78 (0.66 to 0.90), public stigma 0.95 (0.82 to 1.07; means 50.59 vs 42.15), blame subscale (genetic or disease attribution) −0.35 (−0.47 to −0.23), all meaningful by the study's rule; prognostic optimism −0.06 (equivalent); continued care 0.09 (inconclusive); reward −0.03 (equivalent; 248.11 vs 249.72 pence); punishment 0.14 (0.02 to 0.26; inconclusive: the interval does not include zero but reaches below the 0.20 bound; 62.05 vs 53.96 pence). 'Chronically relapsing brain disease' vs 'problem' (392 vs 423, drug-use arm): blame subscale 0.54 (0.38 to 0.71; means 8.61 vs 7.22), meaningful; continued care 0.01 (equivalent); social distance −0.20 (−0.36 to −0.03), prognostic optimism −0.07, danger −0.11, public stigma −0.18 (−0.34 to −0.02; means 49.62 vs 51.20) and reward 0.15, all inconclusive; punishment 0.007 (equivalent). Treatment framed as likely to succeed vs uncertain (383 vs 362): every self-report measure and reward inconclusive (for example public stigma 0.31, 0.14 to 0.48, higher with the uncertain framing), punishment equivalent. Detectable equivalence bounds ±0.28 and ±0.30 for the label and treatment comparisons. Kelly & Westerhoff (2010), label version vs 'substance use disorder' version: 'perpetrator-punishment' subscale 2.92 (SD 0.57) vs 2.82 (SD 0.58) on a 1–6 scale, t = 2.05, 504 df, p printed as .02 (one-sided by the editors' calculation; two-sided about .041), d printed as 0.20 (about 0.17 to 0.18 recomputed; approximate 95% CI 0.01 to 0.36, editors' calculation); 'social threat' (willingness for social contact) and 'victim-treatment' subscales, no difference (ps > .59).
